what_its_for: Prednisolone is a steroid medicine that reduces swelling, redness, and irritation in your body. It is used to treat many conditions including allergies, asthma, arthritis, skin problems, eye conditions, certain blood disorders, and problems with your immune system. Your doctor may prescribe it for other conditions as well.
how_to_take: Take prednisolone exactly as your doctor tells you. It comes as a tablet, a liquid solution, or a dissolving tablet. Always take it with food or milk to help protect your stomach. If you are taking the liquid form, use the measuring cup or spoon that comes with the medicine — do not use a regular kitchen spoon. If you are taking it once a day, try to take it in the morning with breakfast. Swallow tablets whole with a full glass of water. Do not stop taking this medicine suddenly without talking to your doctor first, especially if you have been taking it for more than a few weeks — stopping too quickly can make you feel very sick.
dosing: Your dose depends on your condition, your weight, and how your body responds to the medicine. Doses can range from 5 mg to 60 mg or more per day. Your doctor may start you on a higher dose and slowly lower it over time. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions. Do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store prednisolone tablets at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture — do not store it in the bathroom. Liquid forms may need to be kept in the refrigerator — check the label or ask your pharmacist. Keep this medicine in its original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use medicine that is past its expiration date.
what_to_avoid: Avoid being around people who are sick with contagious illnesses like chickenpox, measles, or the flu, because prednisolone can weaken your immune system and make it harder for your body to fight infections. Do not drink alcohol while taking this medicine, as it can increase the risk of stomach problems and other side effects. Avoid getting live vaccines (such as the chickenpox or shingles vaccine) while on this medicine without talking to your doctor first. Avoid eating large amounts of salty foods, as prednisolone can cause your body to hold onto extra salt and water.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you experience any of the following: signs of infection such as fever, chills, or sore throat; unusual weight gain or swelling in your feet or ankles; vision changes or eye pain; mood changes, depression, or feeling confused; severe stomach pain, black or tarry stools, or vomiting blood; muscle weakness; increased thirst or urination; skin changes such as easy bruising, slow wound healing, or stretch marks; or if you feel extremely tired or weak. If you have a serious allergic reaction — such as trouble breathing, swelling of your face or throat, or severe rash — call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room immediately.
when_it_works: How quickly prednisolone works depends on what condition it is treating. For some conditions like severe allergic reactions or asthma flares, you may start to feel better within a few hours to a day. For other conditions like arthritis or inflammatory diseases, it may take several days to notice improvement. Keep taking your medicine as directed even if you feel better, and do not stop without your doctor's approval.
special_populations: Children: Prednisolone can affect growth in children if used for a long time. The doctor will use the lowest effective dose and monitor your child's growth regularly. Older adults: Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects such as bone loss (osteoporosis), high blood pressure, and blood sugar changes. Your doctor may check your bone density and other health markers. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Talk to your doctor before taking prednisolone if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. It may be used when the benefits outweigh the risks, but your doctor will guide you. Diabetes: Prednisolone can raise your blood sugar levels. If you have diabetes, monitor your blood sugar more closely and let your doctor know if your readings are higher than usual. Kidney or liver problems: Your doctor may need to adjust your dose if you have kidney or liver disease.
